pages.x: By the 1260s Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, ruler of Gwynedd in the mountains of north Wales, had made himself master of most of Wales, and in 1267 the English king recognised him as Prince of Wales. But when Edward I came to the throne, Llywelyn refused, again and again, to come and swear homage to him.

In 1277 Edward invaded from three sides, the king himself marching along the north coast from Chester, cutting roads through the forests as he went. His fleet seized Anglesey and its harvest, the bread of Gwynedd, and the starving Welsh made peace. Llywelyn was left only the land west of the River Conwy.

In 1282 Llywelyn's brother Dafydd stormed the English castle of Hawarden, and all Wales rose. Edward came back, meaning to finish it this time. But an English force crossing a bridge of boats from Anglesey to the mainland was caught by the Welsh at Moel-y-Don, and many knights drowned.

In December Llywelyn went south to raise mid Wales. On 11 December 1282, near Builth, he was killed in a skirmish, cut down, it seems, by an English soldier who did not know who he was. His head was sent to London and set on the Tower, crowned with ivy.

Edward fought on through the winter. His armies took the last Welsh castles, and in June 1283 Dafydd was caught in the mountains. He was hanged, drawn and quartered at Shrewsbury, one of the first men known to have suffered that death.

To hold Wales, Edward built a ring of great stone castles, at Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech and Beaumaris, designed by a master mason from Savoy, James of St George, with walled towns beside them for English settlers. Caernarfon's banded walls were meant to recall those of Constantinople.

By the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284 Wales was annexed to the English crown and divided into shires. In 1301 Edward made his son, born at Caernarfon, Prince of Wales. Ever since, the title has gone to the heir to the English, and later British, throne.

Independent Welsh rule was over. There would be one more great rising, led by Owain Glyndŵr from 1400, but Wales stayed under English rule. Its language and poetry lived on, and Llywelyn is remembered as Llywelyn the Last.
